records.name: Sarawak
records.current_summary:
Same-sex conduct is criminalised federally (penal-code provisions carrying up to 20 years' imprisonment and caning), legal gender recognition is unavailable, and a dual court system applies Sharia jurisdiction to Muslims only, while no federal law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

A 2022 Human Rights Watch report documents state religious authorities harassing LGBT activists and organisations and raiding private events across the federation. The audited sources document no Sarawak-specific enforcement pattern, so the national framework governs what a visitor encounters here.

sources.claim: Human Dignity Trust Malaysia country profile (last updated 16 Dec 2025): the federal Penal Code 1936 criminalises 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature' and acts of 'gross indecency' with up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping, while state Sharia enactments criminalise same-sex intimacy and 'cross-dressing' for Muslims only; no legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded and discrimination and violence against LGBT people are regularly reported, with transgender people particularly vulnerable. Enforcement documented: since the 2018 election a crackdown has been underway — Oct 2022 raid on a Queer Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur with at least 20 LGBT people arrested, an August raid on an LGBT venue with twenty men arrested, a Terengganu Sharia court ordering a lesbian couple caned, and Nov 2023 Johor plans for conversion-therapy centres. The national framework governs what a visitor faces in Sarawak.

Human Rights Watch / Justice for Sisters news release, 10 Aug 2022, on the report 'I Don't Want to Change Myself — Anti-LGBT Conversion Practices, Discrimination, and Violence in Malaysia': 73 LGBT people interviewed across Malaysia 2018-2021; documents the federal penal code punishing oral and anal sex with up to 20 years in prison and government-run 'rehabilitation' programmes that at least 1,733 people had attended as of June 2021. The report names no Sarawak-specific enforcement case; the national crackdown framework applies here.

records.name: Altai Krai
records.current_summary: This division was covered by the dedicated country dossier, which identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately (±0.02); it is therefore assessed at the national score.

sources.claim: UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity (June 2025, assessment updated 11 Jun 2025): same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, gender-marker changes on documents are prohibited, trans people cannot adopt or foster, trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, and no legislation prohibits SOGI-based discrimination in housing, healthcare or employment. Publicly 'promoting' non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is an administrative offence (fines or detention up to 15 days; repeat offences can become criminal, up to 4 years), the 2023 'extremist' designation of the international LGBT+ movement criminalises support/activity, and at least 139 people were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws 2022-2024. Assesses LGB people generally face no real risk of state persecution on orientation alone, except in the North Caucasus — a zone that does not include Altai Krai; this is the national baseline the record stands assessed at.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (Cloudflare block); the underlying US State Department advisory for Russia states that foreigners found guilty of violating the 'propaganda' law may be arrested and detained for up to 15 days and then deported, and that displaying certain symbols including the rainbow flag is a crime; it also advises against all travel to Russia.

Human Rights Watch (30 Jun 2025): Russian courts have issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions over alleged participation in the 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its symbols (about 98 administrative); since January 2024, 81 people in 98 court cases were found guilty of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying symbols such as the rainbow flag, and between Jan 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges for alleged participation — one died by suicide in pretrial detention, two were sentenced to prison, 17 cases pending or unknown. On 15 May 2025 investigators charged three staff of two publishing houses under article 282.2 with running an 'extremist organisation' over selling fiction exploring LGBT themes; they face up to 12 years in prison. National enforcement regime applying equally in Altai Krai; no Altai Krai-specific case is reported in the piece.
